tier_reason: The README (Background section) states libjpeg-turbo is 'generally 2-6x as fast as libjpeg, all else being equal' with no machine, compiler or libjpeg version; the measured tables live on libjpeg-turbo.org/About/Performance, which is blocked here and seen only as a search snippet, so the first-party claim stays C. The benchmark tool itself (src/tjbench.c) is public, but the methodology page could not be opened.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'generally 2-6x as fast as libjpeg, all else being equal' on systems with SIMD; on other systems it 'can still outperform libjpeg by a significant amount' thanks to optimized Huffman coding. ChangeLog.md (1.5 beta1, AltiVec SIMD): compression about 3-4x and decompression about 2-2.5x faster relative to libjpeg v6b on PowerPC. Search snippet only (libjpeg-turbo.org/About/Performance, blocked): 2.1-6.0x as fast as libjpeg across platforms; versus libjpeg v6b 3.47-6.00x for compression and 2.08-3.43x for decompression on x86-64 Linux, measured with tjbench (Mpixels/sec) using a TurboJPEG wrapper built against libjpeg v6b and v8d.
corrections.caveats: First-party claim. The detailed tables (machines, compilers, libjpeg v6b and v8d baselines measured with tjbench through a TurboJPEG wrapper) are on https://libjpeg-turbo.org/About/Performance, which is blocked from this environment, so the per-platform numbers come from a search snippet only and were not checked against the page. libjpeg-turbo is itself one of this category's listed baselines; it is recorded here against the IJG libjpeg incumbent it replaced (zlib-ng precedent). The 2-6x figure dates from the libjpeg v6b/v8 era and says nothing about how it compares with newer decoders. Independent runs that do not use IJG libjpeg as baseline: gereoffy/jpeg-nitro README table (Intel i9 13th gen) has libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 (AVX2) at 124 ms per image versus stb_image 175 ms and Wuffs 159 ms; google/decoder-benchmarks-for-rust (2.6 GHz 6-core Intel Core i7, macOS) has turbojpeg at 84.25 ms versus the Rust jpeg-decoder crate at 126.2 ms on venice-2000x3000.jpg. LICENSE.md now describes two licenses (IJG for the libjpeg API library, Modified BSD for TurboJPEG) with SIMD code under Zlib and components under libpng-2.0 and BSD-2-Clause; the README still says three.

notes: README claim confirmed verbatim; tier C kept because the methodology page (libjpeg-turbo.org) is blocked and no reachable mirror exists in the libjpeg-turbo GitHub organization. License left as recorded; the IJG license is permissive but its OSI status could not be checked (opensource.org blocked). Metadata confirmed: 4.4k stars, last commit 2026-09-25, not archived.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the repo's own README (tags v9.0.0 through v10.0.0; removed at HEAD in favor of the op111 link) carries a hyperfine benchmark against OptiPNG 0.7.7 with the exact commands, a public test image (tests/files/rgb_16_should_be_grayscale_8.png), commit c16519b, rustc 1.74.0-nightly (7b4d9e155 2023-09-28), the release profile in Cargo.toml at that commit (lto = "thin") and an Intel Core i7-12700, so code, compiler, flags and CPU model are all public. The independent op111.net blog the record cited is blocked and was seen only as a search snippet.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README benchmark (tags v9.0.0 through v10.0.0): Oxipng 9.0.0 versus OptiPNG 0.7.7 on one test image, hyperfine wall clock, Intel Core i7-12700: default level 59.6 ms versus 132.4 ms ('2.22 +/- 0.29 times faster'); -o4 88.7 ms versus 444.9 ms ('5.01 +/- 0.25 times faster'). CPU time is closer at -o4: user 270.3 ms versus 444.8 ms, about 1.65x (derived from page data). Older run in the same README (oxipng 5.0.0, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, rustc 1.55.0-nightly): 1.97x at default and 5.16x at -o4. Independent op111.net blog, search snippet only: d3js.org.png default oxipng 0.764 s for 29.14% reduction versus optipng 2.638 s for 25.42% (about 3.5x, derived from snippet data); powertoys.png 0.266 s for 17.62% versus 0.960 s for 5.85% (about 3.6x, derived from snippet data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Oxipng: rustc 1.74.0-nightly (7b4d9e155 2023-09-28), cargo release profile from Cargo.toml at commit c16519b (lto = "thin", strip = "symbols", default opt-level 3), default features including parallel (rayon). OptiPNG 0.7.7 as packaged by Debian unstable (distribution build flags).
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-12700 (8 performance cores, 4 efficiency cores, 20 threads), DDR5-5200 dual channel, Linux 6.5.0-2-amd64 (README run); op111 blog hardware unknown (page blocked).
corrections.workload: hyperfine wall-clock time to optimize one repository test PNG (tests/files/rgb_16_should_be_grayscale_8.png) without writing output (oxipng -P versus optipng -simulate) at the default level and at -o4; the independent op111.net blog adds web images (d3js.org.png, powertoys.png) at default and maximum settings.
corrections.caveats: Rust, not C++ (the search's C++ language filter does not match); OptiPNG is not one of the category's listed baselines (libjpeg-turbo, libpng, libwebp, libavif). The README benchmark is first-party, uses a single small test image, does not report output sizes, and was removed from the README after v10.0.0 in favor of a link to the op111.net blog. Most of the wall-clock gain comes from multithreading on a 20-thread CPU against single-threaded OptiPNG (user CPU time at -o4 is only about 1.65x lower); oxipng also uses libdeflate and its own trial heuristics, so -o4 does not run the same trial set as optipng -o 4 (different work, not an identical algorithm made faster). The README names Oxipng 9.0.0 but Cargo.toml at the cited commit still says 8.0.0. The op111.net numbers are snippet only (page blocked); per the snippet oxipng also compresses better at default settings.

tier_reason: README Benchmarks table matches the record exactly (qoi.h 282.9/225.3 Mp/s versus qoi-rust 427.4/290.0 Mp/s decode/encode) and the harness is public (bench/src/main.rs; qoi.h built at -O3 by libqoi/build.rs), but rustc version, C compiler and the Rust build profile are not stated, so it falls short of A; first-party, so C.

corrections.workload: Encode and decode of 2846 PNG images from the upstream QOI benchmark suite (1.32 GPixels, 4.46 GB of raw pixels), via the repo's bench/src/main.rs: per image and codec, repeated timed encodes and decodes filling a default 1-second budget (at least 2 runs each), median by default, with a round-trip pixel check; totals are sums of per-image medians.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: qoi.h (phoboslab/qoi submodule at 8d35d93) compiled by the cc crate at opt_level 3 with QOI_NO_STDIO and QOI_IMPLEMENTATION (libqoi/build.rs); rustc version, C compiler and Rust build profile not stated.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 129 stars; crates.io crate qoi with 68.4M downloads (17.4M recent)
corrections.caveats: Rust, not C++ (the search's C++ language filter does not match). An independent safe-Rust re-implementation of the QOI format, not an FFI binding or wrapper of qoi.h, so like wx257osn2/qoixx it can sit beside phoboslab/qoi rather than fold into it as a duplicate. Baseline is the QOI reference qoi.h (commit 8d35d93), not a listed category baseline (libjpeg-turbo, libpng, libwebp, libavif). First-party numbers from one Apple M1 laptop with no rustc or C compiler version. By default the encoder emits QOI_OP_INDEX instead of a length-1 QOI_OP_RUN where allowed, so its byte stream can differ from qoi.h's (same size, still valid QOI; the 'reference' feature restores identical output), and each codec decodes its own encoder's output. The README says it is the fastest of the Rust QOI crates but gives no table for the others. The crates.io release (0.4.1) dates from 2022-10-16.

notes: Numbers verified on the README; the record's 'single run per codec' was wrong (the harness repeats and takes medians) and is corrected. Not a duplicate under the qoixx precedent, but flag the Rust language mismatch. Metadata confirmed: MIT OR Apache-2.0, 129 stars, last commit 2025-07-27 (stale), not archived.
